utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin. Good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can, and I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radislav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, David Cunningham with Barbara Baruch, and we're here also with Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you, too. First I would like to inform you and enter into the records that today we are sitting without Judge Taya, who, for urgent personal reasons and reasons which have been authorised -- which have been acknowledged by myself and also the President of the Tribunal, is unable to be with us. Therefore, in virtue of Rule 15 bis(A)(i) and (ii), with the remaining Judges of this Chamber, we are ordering that the hearing of this case continues in the absence of Judge Taya, for not more than five working days as envisaged under the same Rule. So any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, only this: That Your Honours will recall that I asked last week to sit all day today and all day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because of the witness who had problems with his work. In fact, we've now arranged so there's an alteration of the witness order, that he comes next Monday. He just needs to be here for one day. So tomorrow, the next witness will be Mr. Kaiser. I've happily spoken to Mr. Cunningham, who tells me that it's more than likely that he won't require the whole day for Mr. Hidic, nor indeed for Mr. Kaiser. But if necessary, could we just sit a little longer to finish Mr. Kaiser? After that, we can go back to half days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I take it today we will be sitting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 9.00 until 12.30, as I understand it, and then 2.00 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2.00 to 4.00. Okay. That's agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's agreed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And tomorrow we'll be sitting the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, if we could, Your Honour. I know Mr. Kaiser is a very busy man, so he'll be anxious to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we'll try and finish with Mr. Kaiser tomorrow, even if it means sitting for a while longer if necessary. Perhaps, Madam Chuqing, you will make arrangements, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other thing Your Honour asked was for a witness list to the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's been dealt with effectively over the weekend. We will in fact be filing a motion in respect of part of it, but it will be ready for Your Honours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Let's bring Mr. Hidic in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Hidic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please stand up. And before we proceed, may I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration that you made last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that -- can you check -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please stand up and read out again once more the solemn declaration. Thank you. And then we can proceed with the testimony. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I begin this morning by sorting out the confusion I caused myself towards the end of the hearing last Thursday in respect of documents, whether there are three, in fact three -- I'm sorry - two versions of one and as we're going to discover, three of another. Could Your Honours please look at Exhibit P245, which is behind divider 27 in the bundle, and you'll need to look at the original B/C/S version. And could the witness, which I don't think the witness does need to have it. It's just for our purposes. If you look at the page, the last page of the B/C/S, you'll see there are two typed signatures, but only one actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner, because I have the wrong -- I'm sorry. I was -- yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I was getting confused. I didn't see the document straight away, but it is here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, attached to Mr. Hidic's statement was a -- the same document that he provided when the investigator saw him. I'm going to ask that he be handed that now. It may well be we've got a copy that we can ... The English is identical, but as we'll see, Your Honour, the B/C/S is not, although ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, on that document can you see your writing again?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I have it for a moment? Your Honour, it's my fault. He was handed P245. And we'll hand them to Your Honours at the same time. It's for the witness, and then we have copies for Your Honours and for the Registry. All right. We're handing in a number of copies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Could we get a copy of that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, if you turn, please, to the parts of the original, which is in your own language. I think if you go for about four pages, you'll see. Now, in that copy, do you see your writing and underlining?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if Your Honours go to the last page, Your Honours will see that there is -- the difference is that on this copy of it, there's two typed signatures and two handwritten, and on the other there's only one handwritten. Your Honour, may I ask that that version, produced by Mr. Hidic, becomes P245.1, A for the English, B for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was asked whether this is the only difference, that there is -- I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Except that in the last paragraph had been completed and concluded - here it is - had been exhausted and concluded. That's the only thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that is different. Otherwise it's a replication of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I think we've been through before, translation is an art form rather than a science form, so sometimes different words will appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise the substance seems to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'm afraid there's one more document. In fact, if you turn in the bundle to the next document, which is P1833 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For that, we've already produced two versions of it - sorry. I beg your pardon. Well, I must have -- I'm afraid that we've maybe got ourselves -- we seem to have produced this document. I'm not sure why, 1877.3. But Your Honour, 1877.3 -- oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we have this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm now getting confused. It's Monday morning. Can Your Honours look, please, first of all, at 1833.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is behind divider 28. Mr. Hidic -- we've already got two versions of that. Your Honour will recall the signatures were different; we went through that. Mr. Hidic actually brought up yet a third version we've discovered by checking the documents he brought, which is again slightly different. Your Honour, obviously I wouldn't trouble with all this were it not for the fact of this sort of blanket allegation that anything that emanates from AID is a forgery or may be a forgery. Can we just hand up the third version, then? I think that's all we need to do. I think by mistake we've produced it as 1877. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is 1877.1 and 1877.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in fact, it's my error, Your Honour, because it's the same document with different versions as 1833.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one is the same document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was produced as -- 1877 is the same document as 1833.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this: 1877.1 is certainly not the same in the full sense of the meaning as 1833.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the same document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but -- oh, I see. You mean the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The B/C/S version may be -- yes. Let me check, because ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at it, it's the minutes from the 35th session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes. But it's -- well, I look at 1877.1, the green, and I look at 1833, the B/C/S version. The top left corner --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Says 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is 57 -- it's not in the green one that I am seeing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. But if you read the text, it's identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would imagine so, except that I can't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honours look -- I mean, it's the 35th session held at 17 -- at 1920 minutes thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not, Ms. Korner. It's -- the text is identical, but the signatures are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, that's what I'm trying to do, put together -- the text is identical, the signatures -- not all of them are. Right. There are three versions of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first is the one provided to us by AID, and that is Exhibit P1833.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second is the one that I produced yesterday -- Thursday, which was given by Mr. Hidic, who brought it with him the day before he -- or the day he came here, and then he provided us with an earlier version, which again is marginally different, which I just want to exhibit now, on the signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is 1877.2 as well, which is the same document but again the order of the signatures is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Well, Your Honour, can I just then -- I think we had better leave the exhibit number as it is, otherwise we're all going to get very confused. But the versions 8 -- P1877.1, 2, and 3, all which are slightly different in the signatures, are all produced by Mr. Hidic, I hope. And we'll hand in now this version. And having now confused everybody on a Monday morning -- sorry. I think perhaps Mr. Hidic had better just identify again his writing on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't have -- are you circulating 1877.3 now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am. And I'm just going to get Mr. Hidic in a moment to identify his writing on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This has one signature less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And as Your Honours just said, the difference here is it's one signature less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, again, is this a document that you were provided with by someone who had access to the municipal building, and you've written on it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document that I had with me and that I handed over to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, that becomes 1877.3. Your Honour, just so there's no confusion, although Mr. Hidic's documents, where they are the same as provided by AID are the same in terms of the text, they're all different. None of them are identical. And for the most part, the documents he's provided do not have a corresponding one from AID.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Sorry about that, Mr. Hidic. We just had to sort out your documents. Now, Mr. Hidic, I want to go back, finally, to the events that took place in Petrovac. I want to deal with what happened to property in Bosanski Petrovac. Can I just for a moment check a document we've already looked at. Yes. During the period before the expulsion, from about April of 1992, did anything happen to homes and businesses owned by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just describe to us briefly what that was.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, in late May, once the blockade of the road towards Bihac was lifted, this coincided with the developments in Bosanski Petrovac municipality. That involved Muslims, that is, Bosniaks. On the 28th of May, there was an attack on a Bosniak house, the house owned by Atif Redzic. The attack was by a hand-held rocket launcher and chemical weapons. On the following morning, like the majority of the citizens of Bosanski Petrovac, I came there, and I saw that the house had been shelled and that the shells had a chemical content, because one could smell some very bad odours, and I also saw a group of political representatives of the authorities of Bosanski Petrovac. I also saw the police, and they were talking to the people, explaining to them what had happened and answering their questions. Soon after that, in June, sometime around the 2nd of June, there was another attack on the part of the town inhabited by Muslims. On the 4th of June, we witnessed the first victims of an attack. A person was killed in front of the Alpina coffee bar sometime before the curfew, an hour before the curfew, Muhamed Terzic was killed. Later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come on with the killings in a moment. I just want to deal with the attacks on property, if I may.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The property was also targeted. First there were attacks on Bosniak business premises and craft shops which were in the centre of the town. Within one week, the total assets of Bosniaks that used to be their property before that was destroyed. All these attacks would usually happen during the night, during the curfew and all these attacks were carried out by hand grenades. There were traces to that effect, and every -- and I personally visited the barber shop that had been destroyed on the previous night. I believe that the police came. This was my brother-in-law's barber shop. I believe that they collected the remains of the hand grenade. My brother-in-law did some repairs on that same day, but on that same evening another attack ensued. This time -- this not involved hand grenades, but an automatic rifle, by which the glass was shattered and everything in the shop was destroyed. So as I've said, within the space of one week between the 5th or the 6th of June and the 15th of June, all the Bosniak shops and business premises in the town were destroyed, not only in the town but also in its vicinity. In the meantime, there were also cases of cars being confiscated, lorries being confiscated. Allegedly, they were confiscated because the army ordered their confiscation or mobilisation. At some occasions, some papers were even produced; however, the luxurious cars were mostly confiscated by force, at gun point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've described how on a number of occasions when you arrived the police were there. To your knowledge, was anybody ever caught or prosecuted for any of these offences?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing. I really am not, during those days. The police did indeed come and investigate. They even took pictures, these shops that were damaged. But I'm not aware of any criminal charges being brought against the perpetrators of this nighttime vandalism.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were there any mosques in the town of Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course. There were some in Bosanski Petrovac, in the very centre of town, and also in the wider area of town. There were two mosques. And there was a third one, in the village of Rasinovac. And the fourth one was in Bjelaj. Since the Second World War, it hadn't been repaired until the other war broke out, and it did not have a minaret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to the mosques?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two mosques in town, during the month of July, during the night between the 7th and the 8th, and the 8th and the 9th, were totally destroyed. They were blown up. The minaret was blown up. And as the mosque was blown up, the roof and the walls were damaged. Over 50 per cent, 60 per cent, that's the extent to which the facility itself was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when did those -- at what time of day did this destruction take place?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first mosque was destroyed around 12.00, between 12.00 and 1.00, and the other one also sometime within that time frame, around 1.00, perhaps a bit after 1.00. I cannot recall with any precision now. But it is in that period, at that time, that both mosques in town were blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's in the early hours of the morning, then, or do you mean during the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After midnight. After midnight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you very briefly, please, to look at Exhibit P1863, which is the last one in the binder. And could you turn in that, please, to the paragraph number 4, the big paragraph, which should be headed "Information on Destroyed Buildings by Location." It's on the fifth page, I think, of your version. Now, this is a report prepared by the Bosniaks in 1997, and so obviously it includes everything that happened until the end of the war. But we see here that in the town area, 545 buildings owned by Muslims were destroyed, with the following degrees of destruction. By the time you left Bosanski Petrovac, in September 1992, how many houses had actually been destroyed, that you can now recall, roughly?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of a few buildings having been torched. They burned down, of course. And afterwards it was cleared up by way of people carrying out work obligation. These are buildings that are in town. But I also know that a large number of old Bosnian buildings that were primarily not inhabited, they were also torched in September 1992. But I think that what is shown here -- I mean, most of the damage was caused the war itself. That is to say, at the time when we were not in Bosanski Petrovac itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But then going to, please, the information on the cultural and religious facilities, which is the next big paragraph, 5. If you go to religious facilities, there were four mosques in the municipality, and then over the page, it lists three mosques that were demolished. Were all those mosques that you know about destroyed before you left, as you've described to us, in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can give that document back now -- actually, no, keep that document for a moment, because I want to move to killings, and I want to take this, if I can, shortly by using the documents. At the front of this document, there are a list of people who have been killed and are buried. And could you take also, please, Exhibit P1878, which is the report from the expatriate club that was in Zagreb, which you've read before. In both those reports, there are descriptions of killings that took place, and you began to describe to us the killing of a person who was outside a shop. Having read both these reports, are those descriptions first of the killings which took place in -- shown in the expatriate document, P1878? Is that an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It concerns the first killing, and the description of that killing is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you can see -- well, I'm sorry. I'm going to stop there. Did you personally witness any of these killings that took place in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was very hard to be an eyewitness, because this happened during the night, that is to say, during the curfew, which I think was imposed only upon the Muslims, or rather, the Bosniaks. How should I put this? As for the Serb population, life went on as usual. But at any rate, in the morning, people would find out about what had happened, and many of these killings could be seen by a large number of citizens. Inter alia, I saw some of the killings after they had been committed during the night, and sometimes I also attended the funerals of these people who were so unfortunately killed, of course, when it was possible to attend such ceremonies. My experience is related to Osman Hadzic, my neighbour who was also killed, but he was killed in the period between the 20th and 24th of September. Of course, I saw his corpse. He was shot in the head with two bullets. The police was there, on site, on site. They carried out an on-site investigation. They made it possible for us, through Mico Atlagic, Milovan Atlagic, my neighbour - his name has already been mentioned here - that we try to bury the body within 15 or 20 minutes. There were very few of us, only three or four. I can't remember exactly. But in the garden right behind their house, we managed to dig a shallow grave and to bury the remains in that grave. Of course, this was risky. It was risky to do this kind of thing, because during those days, at any moment, a patrol could show up, and their exclusive task was to patrol the Muslim-populated areas of Bosanski Petrovac. Of course, they would open fire against any person who would be outside their houses. They would even kill people who would be seen that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you had to bury people after the curfew?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was during the day. The burial took place during the day, around noon or in the afternoon. I can't remember exactly, but it took quite a while for the police to come. Of course, before that, they carried out the identification, and only then the on-site investigation took place by the police, and then only later did they ask to have it buried. The corpse could not be taken to the cemetery, of course, but it had to be buried somewhere around the house, so it was buried in the garden, as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me just pick up on that. Why couldn't it go to the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was impossible because of the patrols. I already mentioned that the patrols were circulating, and this infamous white Golf, as it was called, it was driving around the Muslim neighbourhoods, and whenever they would see any signs of life in yards or in the street, they would open fire. There was absolute fear, and it was impossible to carry out the burial at the local cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This infamous white Golf, who were the people who were driving around in it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, they were younger people, and it was very hard to establish their identity. However, people did mention some names, but I cannot confirm this myself. I personally saw the Golf, but I did not see the people who were sitting in the Golf and who were shooting from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Leave aside their names for the moment. Were the people who were in the Golf and shooting at Muslims, were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in uniform. They were in uniform. That could be seen. They had olive-green/grey shirts or T-shirts and of course you couldn't see any caps on their head. They looked like any soldier in the world to me. I mean, when you see them in such uniform, it was very hard to tell them apart. And you didn't really have the opportunity of seeing this very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were the uniforms like official police uniforms or different?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think they wore different clothing, but I think they preferred olive-grey. More were in olive-grey. It was fashionable to wear Rambo-style clothes with short sleeves, and of course young soldiers tried to emulate that, especially in situations like this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the first killing was of this man called Muhamed Terzic, outside -- you were starting to tell us, outside a bar. Were you actually present when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, I was not present. Hardly anyone was present, because before that, in the direction of the Alpina cafe that is, say, about 300 to 500 metres away from the centre of town, perhaps a bit more than that - I cannot be very accurate right now - shooting went on all the time. They were even shooting at houses that were owned by Muslims. And then - I don't know how this happened, but a man happened to be there in the street. But at any rate, I later find out - people talked about this - that he was in the company of a young man, a Serb, a former colleague of his, and they were probably together. And it is quite certain that this man had guaranteed his safety. However, what proved to be fateful was that this young man ran away, because the shooting started. So he remained on his own, and of course they did all sorts of things to him and then ultimately killed him in front of Alpina, right there on the sidewalk. This could be seen in the morning, the place where he had been killed. Of course, the corpse had been collected by then, but there was a small pool of blood there where he had been killed. People could come and they could see the actual site where this took place, but it would be noteworthy to mention that at Terzic's funeral there were Bosniak Muslims but there were also a large number of Serbs who were present and who were shocked in this way by the vandalism that had occurred in Bosanski Petrovac. It's not only that the killing took place -- that this killing took place that night, but another one, Sead Husagic's killing took place. It was far worse than that. I've already described that a few days ago. Rifle grenades were thrown at his house and they had some chemical components too. And he happened to be in his yard, looking for his dog that was not on his leash, and these men saw him and they shot him. I mean, they were shooting in this Muslim neighbourhood anyway, and when they noticed him, they caught up with him, they dragged him out into the street, they beat him first, then they wounded him in the leg so he could not run away. And after this dramatic beating and his screams that were heard by the neighbours but regrettably nobody dared go out to help the unfortunate Sead, the same evening, when the family appealed, the representatives of the police came, put him in a car and took him to the medical centre, the health centre, which is close to his house, and two days later he succumbed to his very grave wounds. He died. There was a funeral afterwards and many citizens attended the funeral, Bosniaks and Serbs, and the comments were such that they actually amounted to bitterness. How could something like that happen in a town like Bosanski Petrovac? Until then, everybody kept saying that nothing would happen there, that such things could not happen there, that people could not be killed in the street just like that. The same night there was shooting at the houses and shops of Bosniak Muslims. A woman was seriously wounded then, and along with her child. Her child was about 6 or 7 years old. They were both seriously wounded and they were transferred to the health centre the same night. They were given assistance there and then they were released the very next day. They were told that they could not be kept at the health centre but they said that the wounded were being brought in and that nobody could guarantee anything anymore and they were released. They were sent home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How shortly after those incidents had taken place were you told about them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically the same day, the same morning, people found out about this. People could come freely and see this. I mean, the places where these things had happened. As a matter of fact, there were some traces in the street itself. A bottle with an alcoholic drink. It was not empty, so it was probably the people who had done this that had been drinking. After we left, of course, I found out about this after returning to Bosanski Petrovac. I found out that this was done by Mico Basta, nicknamed Rambo, from Krnjeusa, a Serb village not far away, or rather 20 kilometres away from Bosanski Petrovac, halfway between Bosanski Petrovac and Bosanska Krupa. Some other people from the village of Krnjeusa were with him. I don't know how many. But it is known that an attempt was made to disarm this Mico Rambo and this proved to be unsuccessful. As far as I know, he is a free man still in Republika Srpska. He was never held accountable for the crimes that he had committed in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've already told us about somebody being beaten before he was killed. Were there beatings that took place in Petrovac of Bosniaks, without people being killed as a result?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. Before this beating, there were beatings by policemen and people were taken out of town. Perhaps even a month before this, people were physically tortured, beaten, but they didn't dare speak about it. It was even made possible for some to free from Bosanski Petrovac after such beatings, and so many people did indeed avail themselves of this opportunity and they went in the direction of Bihac, because that was possible until, say, the 27th or 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want, then, please, to deal with the prisons. We looked at a document yesterday about holding people -- yesterday, on Thursday - about holding people in the SJB. You told us that you had -- you were the manager of a warehouse that was situated outside Bosanski Petrovac. Did you become aware of any prison in that vicinity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I've already told you that I worked in Bosnaplast. This is just outside the town zone, on the road between Bosanski Petrovac and Drvar, and already in 1991, there was a logistical centre that was set up there. Of course, I did not know straight away what this had to do with this logistics centre, but eventually it really did become a centre, because there were more and more men in uniform there. Some people who worked in the factory itself, that is to say, who were reserve officers, were already called up as reservists, and they were there at the logistics centre. I think I mentioned the name of an engineer, a technologist, or rather, a manager in this company, Tomo Miscevic. He was a JNA captain, a reserve captain -- Captain or Captain First Class. It doesn't really matter now. But he does have the rank of captain. And he was one of the leaders of this logistics centre. Of course, there was a kitchen there too. Its objective was to provide supplies to everyone in the field and the area. And later on, this kitchen provided food for the camp that was established sometime in the beginning of July, in Kozila, in the village of Drinic, or rather, above the village of Drinic in the mountain of Klekovaca. I heard of a story, and this version was confirmed later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Confirmed by who, the story you're about to tell us?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was confirmed later, after the liberation, of course, that plans were being made for the prison at the police station, which had become too small for all the persons who had been detained in the meantime, that it should be transferred about 100 to 150 metres away from Bosnaplast, to Kartal's house, his nickname was Pean that two other houses in that area should be empty. One was set fire to and the other was blown up after this, because it was made of some kind of hard material and it couldn't burn down easily. And Mr. Pean's house was supposed to be turned into a prison, since it had a good basement, a good cellar, rather a spacious one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at the document that I think you're referring to. Could you have a look, please, at P1833, which is the one that Mr. Hidic has got the version of, the one we had numbered versions of. It's the Crisis Staff decision number 57 of the 16th of June. And if we look at the top of page 2 in our translation, the man who was head of the police force, Mr. Gacesa, talked about a list of 40 people or so considered to be organisers, a separate group, or to have acted from extreme fundamentalist Islamic position. And then going down that paragraph, there are two possible options, one that a certain number of persons who could be a potential threat be isolated, but not on the premises of the SJB public security station; and the other, that extremists be isolated outside Petrovac. Then, as the discussion continued, the view prevailed that the isolation of extremists outside Petrovac would be dangerous to themselves, and it was best to isolate them in a well-guarded facility on the outskirts of town. And then we see a decision that all individuals who possess illegal weapons or have been registered as Muslim extremists, thus posing a potential threat, shall be detained and held in custody. And then the next paragraph talks about the part that you've just dealt with. And do I understand that you're telling us that you were aware of this because you saw the houses being destroyed, or the house?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This house was not destroyed. It was the two houses next to it that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're quite right. And then the SJB will remove all Muslim owners of weekend cottages from the Ostrelj weekend settlement. Where was that, the weekend settlement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This weekend settlement called Ostrelj is on the road between Bosanski Petrovac and Drvar. We're talking about a mountain area some 1.300 metres high. And previously it was a tourist recreation office or facility. Sometime in the 1980s, a plan was made to transform it into a residential area, or rather, a weekend area. And then sometime in 1984, during the winter Olympic games in Sarajevo, a third ski slope was built there. The first one was in Vlasic, the second one in Ostrelj, and then the one in Bosanski Petrovac. This was a large settlement. I believe that there were between 50 and 100 holiday bungalows, or even more than that. And a number of people of all ethnic backgrounds came to this area for weekends. However, the majority of those weekend houses belonged to the Serbian officer from the Second World War, and some other high officials and prominent politicians and so on and so forth. There was also a number of owners who were of Muslim ethnic background. And those people were from Bosanski Petrovac, Bihac, Banja Luka, and some other towns out of Bosanski Petrovac municipality. They were all completed and they were all inhabited. They all served its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just look, please, for a moment at P1804. We'll just put it up on the ELMO just to identify the map. And can we see there the town you're talking about at the bottom of the map?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And -- thank you. You can give it back to the Usher. All I want to know about then finally is: Do you know whether the Muslim owners of cottages there were removed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During these days, these people did not reside in these cottages. It was already the beginning of a war, so the majority, or rather, none of the Muslims who had their weekend cottages up there did not go there. These houses were vacant. There were no Muslims or anybody there. These houses were used for the accommodation of Serbian officers and Serbian troops who even had their command post up there. And there was a hotel there, a property of the Grmec catering establishment. It had about 30 to 50 beds. And this hotel was also used for accommodation for military purposes. And the hotel -- there was another hotel owned by SIP Ostrelj. It was like a workers holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hidic, but I think that's all I needed to know. But thank you. Okay. Can you please now have a look at P1840. This is a list of people who -- for whom the Petrovac SJB had ordered isolation. And at the bottom, a total of 29 persons were taken to do labour at the Kozila camp on the 1st of July, 1992. First, did you know these people who are named here? We see at number 8 somebody called Muhamed [as interpreted] Hidic. Was that a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my relative and my neighbour. And I am familiar with the majority of these people. These people were first arrested and detained in the police building in Bosanski Petrovac, and later on they were all transferred to the camp in Kozila. All to the last on this list were in the Kozila camp in Bosanski Petrovac. Obviously, this list should be much longer. There were many more people from Bosanski Petrovac, but there were also people from Kljuc, Kulen Vakuf, Orahovac, so from the larger area of Bosanski Petrovac as well, not only from the town of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the camp of Kozila, was that separate from the one you've just been talking about at the Bosnaplast?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no camp at Bosnaplast. It was just a logistical centre. The camp was in Kozila. And before that, the only prison was the police building in Bosanski Petrovac. But when it became too small, then people were transferred to Kozila. Can you please repeat your question? I'm afraid I've lost you for a moment. I don't know what you actually asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry. Again, if I can just remind you, Mr. Hidic, if you'll just answer the question. But I actually asked you whether Kozila was in a separate place from the Bosnaplast facility you described, and you've explained that it was.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can put that document away. Now, I want to move really now to the final moment or time in Petrovac, first of all, and ask you about work obligation. Were you made to do work obligation?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All the people of military age, and this applied to Muslims as well, had to respond to the call-ups. Those call-ups were rather strange. They bore a stamp of the Drvar command, and this caused confusion. However, people were afraid, and they responded to these call-ups and then organised groups which always included some members of Muslims to leave such groups, and these groups were escorted, they were guarded, and they were taken for work. Mostly into the field, to the farms. It was in June and July, the period of farm works. And they also had to dig trenches for the telephone cable from Bosanski Petrovac to Drinic and they also had to dig canals along the facility that was being built by Autotransport Bosanski Petrovac in the vicinity of the town and they were also used for all sorts of loading, unloading, for preparing timber, logs, and the most important thing is that these people were also used for the cleaning of military -- --- Break taken at 10.14 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: For the record, we will resume in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That shows you what a little shrimp can do to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like to tell us which restaurant it was so we don't go there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, I was asking you about work obligation. We already looked at a document in relation to that. But can I ask you in particular, what were you made to do?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had one call-up on the 24th of July, in front of my former company, Bosnaplast. I started from there. We didn't know where we were taken to. There were some 50 of us in a bus. There were also escorts, five military policemen, and there was also a driver. So the total number of people on that bus was around 55, 56. We didn't know where we were being taken, but it was indicated in the call-up paper that we should bring access. On that morning, I responded to that call, although around those days I was not feeling well, in 1991. I had been treated in the hospital in Bihac, and also in Zagreb, at the Jordanovac hospital, where I stayed about a month and I was still undergoing therapy in that particular period of time. So to resume, we went by bus towards Bihac, Vrbas, Krnjeusa, and further on, we took the dirt road towards Bosanska Krupa. As we approached Bosanska Krupa, we took the road towards Veliki Gradic, the road on the left. There the school had been transformed into a barracks and the whole place was, so to say, besieged by the army. I knew most of the troops because they were locals. And it seems that the Bosanski Petrovac units was stationed there. From there, when our escorts received new orders, from there we went towards Mali Radic, towards the front line, the delineation line. We came to the area called Grabez, and that's where we were taken to the front line, where Serbian soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment, please. When you got there, was there any firing or shelling going on?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We heard several grenades being fired, either from a tank or from artillery weapons. That is how much I know about artillery and that type of fire. So we arrived there and we were told to stay on the bus, although it was rather hot. I believe that it was the hottest day in 1992. We waited there for well over two hours, while one of the military policemen went somewhere in a Jeep. And in the meantime, while we were waiting for his return, all of a sudden we could hear a song, shrieks, the sound of an engine. A group of troops came in a Pinzgauer, a military vehicle. They did not wear military uniforms. They wore all sorts of military uniforms. I believe the group numbered up to ten people. Among them I recognised two men that I knew from Bosanski Petrovac. One of them was Mladjo Marjanovic. He drove that vehicle. And there was also Gorinko Jakovljevic, a disabled person who had a congenital disease. I believe that he was a journalist. He had --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I stop you, Mr. Hidic? This is important, but we don't need all the description. Were these two men Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were both Serbs. And those who were with them stormed onto the bus. When they saw the bus and when they saw that they were Muslims, and on that bus they stormed into the bus, they broke -- actually, the door was open, both the front door and the back door were open. One of the guards asked the driver to leave the doors open. They stormed onto the bus. They started forking out their knives, their daggers. They started talking to us. They started saying: Oh, here are the Turks. Let's inspect their passports. Let's see if they have visas. Their voices were really intimidating and the way they talked to us was rather scary. They started asking all sorts of questions. At that moment, I could not pay attention to everything that was going on at the bus, because one of those guys who entered the bus by way of the front door targeted me. I was in the front seat together with another young man. I was next to the window, and this young man was by the passage. And there was a rail in front of us, so I couldn't move. I couldn't go backward, I couldn't go anywhere. They were asking all sorts of questions. They were looking for cigarettes. They wanted to see if anybody had a ring or a necklace or a golden chain. They asked if anybody had money. At that moment, nobody had any valuables on them, because, according to the call-up papers, we all assumed that we would be performing some work, and everybody prepared themselves to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause there, please. All right. You started to tell us one of the people targeted you, one of the people who came onto the bus. What did he do to you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't do anything, but he held a bayonet, a knife, against my breast, and I just remained sitting, at, so to say, at the point of his knife. And thanks to another person who pushed him further into the bus, because he wanted himself to get on to see if there was anybody that he would be interested in, I believe that this saved me, because this second person who got on the bus took a little notebook from his pocket and started asking about different people, different Muslims. And we would then say: No, this person is not here. And then finally he cursed at us and said: How come these people are not on the bus? And then he asked: Well, who are we? Who are you people? Then we said: We are from Bosanski Petrovac. And then he said: Well, that explains why these people that I'm looking for are not here. The policemen who were supposed to guard us did not do their job. They just let these people get on the bus and ill-treat us in different ways and threaten us. They marched through the bus. They collected all of our cigarettes and lighters. That's all that they could take, and then they got off the bus. Later on, one of the people who were on the bus and who were sitting in front, next to me, on the other side, he asked the driver, Mitar Jevic, who was driving the bus, he asked him: How did the policemen allow these people get on the bus and do whatever they wanted to do to us? His answer was: Did you think that we would risk our lives for you? If they got hold of somebody, they would not have stayed alive. So I suppose we were just lucky, and we were saved with the help of a guard. We were not harmed in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And was the end result that you never did any work that day but were just driven back to Petrovac after some hours?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they did not know why we were sent here, why we were brought here. Later on, all sorts of stories were --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about all sorts of stories. All I'm interested in is whether you did any work that day or you were simply driven back to Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were driven back to Bosanski Petrovac, but we were not supposed to get there before 7.00. That's why, on the way back, as we left that road and as we arrived at the road towards Krnjeusa, we were taken off the bus and we had to walk behind the bus for some 20 kilometres or so, because we were not supposed to arrive there before 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is this situation that that was the only day that you personally were asked to do work obligation?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only time that I was asked to do that, and there were a lot of stories about that, and I really, until the very end, until the moment I was expelled from Bosanski Petrovac, was never asked to do any work obligation, but others did go and perform the works that I described to you a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, before I deal with the expulsions, were you yourself ever placed into a detention camp?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How would you describe the town of Bosanski Petrovac during this period, particularly between July and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little while ago you asked me if I was ever at a camp. I said no. But I believe that Bosanski Petrovac and the Muslims in that town, during the period between June and the moment when they were expelled, in September, were all at a camp, because they were restricted in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look, please, now, quickly, at Exhibit P1841, which is a document that you yourself provided to us. If we look at the first page of the copy, does that again contain your writing and underlining?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated the 2nd of July, Crisis Staff minutes, or rather, they were held on the 1st of July, and we see under item 1, a report on the security situation on the territory, assessing it as delicate, with a popular feeling of discontent, especially directed towards Muslims after the recent events on the front line, and stress that the best and a sure solution for the protection of the Muslims would be to move the population, emphasising that the territory of the municipality was large. Now, that's the beginning of July. Were there any expulsions, actual expulsions as opposed to people leaving, during the period of July and August?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we -- thank you very much. And can you look, please, then, at P1843. This is a decision of the Municipal Assembly, the commission for moving out, and on Thursday we looked at the Crisis Staff decision that referred to setting up such a commission, which says that Muslims may move away voluntarily on the following conditions: "If they sign a contract on the exchange of immovable property and if they sign a statement giving their immovable property to the state." And then it sets out further on the actual nuts and bolts, if one likes, of how that's to happen. Now, were you aware and did you yourself eventually have to sign a statement leaving your property to the state.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I was aware of this because this information regarding the exchange arrived via the forum of citizens. They wanted somebody to go to the cadastral office in the municipality, to inspect the land books, and those who in the meantime came in touch with the representatives of the Serbian people who resided on the territory of Bosanski Petrovac municipality, and before that resided in Bihac, in other words, who came from the territory of the municipality of Bihac to Bosanski Petrovac. And this was the alleged contract regarding the exchange of property in Bosanski Petrovac and Bihac. Before they could do that, these people had to settle all of their bills, they had to pay all of their utility bills, they had to pay all their taxes. Once you were given the receipt that all of these debts were settled, you were supposed to go to the police administration. There you would apply for the voluntary relinquishing of all your property in view of leaving Bosanski Petrovac. As of that moment, you stopped being the citizen of the town where you lived, where you were born. It was a common practice. This is what was asked from people, and the majority of the people believed that this should be done in this way. A lot of Bosniaks, a lot of Muslims, subscribed to that. They started looking for partners with whom they would sign the contract. However, such contracts were never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, I'm sorry to stop you like this, but if you'll recall -- if you just answer very simply the question that I ask you, and then if I need more details or the Court does, we'll ask you for more details. The simple question was: Did you have to sign a statement leaving your property to the state?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not a sign such a statement leaving my property to the state, but I had to go to the police administration and release the document on wishing to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you look, please, at a second document, P1844, which is a decision of the 3rd of August of these commissioners. And if you look, please, under the decision, you'll see, just before item AD3, "The commission will establish who can leave the Petrovac municipality, and the condition will be for them to exchange their property or give it to the state," that is, the Serbian municipality of Petrovac. So there were two different methods: One, you could exchange or you could leave, leaving your property to the state. Those who did an exchange, was that with Serbs in Bihac who wished to move to Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those Serbs from Bihac had already arrived in Bosanski Petrovac. That is to say that before the conflict broke out between Bihac and Bosanski Petrovac, I mean before that conflict, they had come to Bosanski Petrovac, not as refugees but at the invitation of the SDS. They left their homes and they came to the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac. And all these talks went in that direction, that is to say, they had to do with exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If an exchange was arranged by a Muslim in Petrovac, with whom would it be arranged, was it arranged?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb from Bihac who was already in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did those exchanges work, as far as the Muslims were concerned? In other words, were the Muslims able to go to Bihac to take up a Serb property?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. In the month of July, it was already impossible to leave, because of the war operations. But by way of lists and by way of these contracts, the departure of Muslims from Bosanski Petrovac to Bihac would be organised into the territory where the property of the Serbs was, that is to say, those Serbs who had arrived in Bosanski Petrovac prior to the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So is what you're saying that on paper there was an exchange, but in reality the Muslims never managed to get to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This was just activity on paper, so to speak, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you just briefly, please, look at 1846, which is two of these types of documents that we've been discussing, or three, I think, actually - four. The first relates to a family named Hodzic, who was going to move out. Then the second to -- oh, it's still the Hodzics, I think, actually, it's about declaring that they owned the property and that they conceded it permanently to the Petrovac Municipal Assembly, and so on and so forth. Do you know this particular family?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I do know this family. This family is from Bjelaj, that is to say, in a neighbourhood that is about 25 kilometres away from Bosanski Petrovac. Muslims, or rather, the Bosniak citizens of this village, stayed on until about the 13th of January. If you look at the date here, that is the 10th of August, that is to say, this was after the expulsion of Muslims from Bosanski Petrovac. This group of Muslims in Bjelaj remained all the way up to the following year, the 13th of January, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is dated the 10th of August, 1992, so that's before.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't see this properly. Yes, it is the 10th of August. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is the period when talks were conducted and when these contracts were being made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you look next, please, at P1848. This document is from the Yugoslav news agency, and this is Mr. Dosen, the gentleman who I think you said you knew; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dosen. And it talks about, on the 13th of September, that "The mass departure of Muslims from the area of Bosanski Petrovac is still continuing. A column of seven buses with a special escort departed from the village of Biscani, in the direction of Travnik. According to information from the Petrovac office for the exchange of population and property, over the last three days, more than 900 men, women, and children of Muslim ethnicity have moved from the area of Petrovac in the direction of Bihac and Travnik." Now, there is a description of this convoy in the document from the expatriate committee, explaining how the convoy in fact was turned back. And if we look at, please, document 1849, which is the next document, there is the description of the Petrovac SJB -- it's the report to the Banja Luka CSB, in fact, to the chief. You've read both these documents. Are those descriptions that are contained in the document, particularly this one, 1849, a fairly accurate description? I don't want to go through it, Mr. Hidic, so if you'd just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that what is written here is absolutely correct. There are some correct assertions, but all of it is not accurate, I mean in relation to Karinovac, when these buses were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Briefly, and I mean briefly, Mr. Hidic, can you tell us what, in your view, is inaccurate. But first of all, can you tell us how you know. Did you know people who were on this convoy?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I found out from these people who were on the second convoy, if I can put it that way. Before that, two buses had left and gone through Vlasic to Travnik. The second one was bigger, that is to say, it involved larger numbers. However, due to the war operations that were taking place during those days at the Vlasic plateau, passage was not possible through Karinovac. This is somewhere at the crossroad on the road between Jajce and Banja Luka, towards Skender Vakuf, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... stop you, Mr. Hidic. Just look at the report and tell us what is inaccurate, as far as you are concerned, from talking people who were on it.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is just a description here of the police administration, or rather, the policemen who gave these people protection, these people who were on the bus. However, there is no mention of how these people were met, how they were intimidated during the night while they were staying in Karinovac. This was done to them not only by the Serb soldiers but also part of the local population. The truth is that this policeman, Ribic, truly accorded full protection in that sense. I can state that. He did protect these people on the bus. But when Radojko came, the situation became even more complicated. If I can put it this way, things became even harder for the people who were on the buses. When he left, it was possible to allow these people to return to Bosanski Petrovac. During the night, during the curfew, they arrived in Bosanski Petrovac. That is where they were when the morning broke, and of course this news spread, like all good news. Now, as for the entire story as to what happened to them on that day in Karinovac, there is only just -- there is just one detail, that they were throwing hand grenades in this bus where they were rolling them on the floor in the bus, where there were women and children, primarily. That is one of the details, I mean as to how these people were mistreated while they were on the buss.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you -- Radojko is a name that we've seen appearing in the minutes of the Crisis Staff meetings. What was his job?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was secretary of the Executive Council. This is a municipal authority. And of course, he was a member of the Executive Board of the SDS of Bosanski Petrovac. As far as I know, he was born in Bosanski Petrovac, somewhere in the surrounding area, but before that, until 1991, they lived in Croatia. He lived in Croatia, in Zagreb. He got a degree in law there, and he was active there and he worked there --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Don't worry about that. I just wanted to know what his job was. I don't want his background as well. Thank you. All right. Can we come, then, please, finally, to your own expulsion. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific answer is the 24th of September, 1992, we had to leave the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac. Of course, this was preceded by very tragic events, very tragic from my point of view. They occurred on the 20th of September. It was a Sunday. We Muslims call it the Black Sunday for the Muslims in Bosanski Petrovac, because on that day, sometime in the evening hours, the news arrived that at the Grmusa front line 17 Serb soldiers were killed and that they were brought before the health centre, and that an alarm was sounded then to those who were free then, soldiers and paramilitaries, that it was a free-for-all in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, that they could do whatever they wanted to the Muslims. And they immediately split up in [Realtime transcript read in error "split up in chiropractors"] troikas as they were called, and they really started carrying out such activities. General panic prevailed, people started running away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We need to make this clear. You say that 17 Serbs were killed at the front line. Was that within the Petrovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this was at the front line, where the front line was, because on that day, these people had been sent --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, please. I want to ask you a series of questions, please. I don't want you to carry on. I just want you to answer these questions, please. First, the front line, you say, was in the Petrovac municipality, front line where in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was not in the municipality of Petrovac. It was far away from the urban area, perhaps some 40 kilometres away. That is Grmusa, the Grabez plateau, in the area between Ripac and Pritoka, where the separation line was. So it was quite far away from the centre of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, next you say that these 17 Serb soldiers were killed. Killed by whom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were killed by sabotage men who got in beyond the separation line, that is to say, further from the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So they were non-Serbs, were they?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Members of the Bosnian army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, who was brought before the health centre, and which health centre?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the health centre in Bosanski Petrovac, and it was the Serb soldiers who had been sent to the front line that morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So they arrived in front of the health centre in Bosanski Petrovac. Then you say that they divided into troikas. Do you mean into threes?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then you say they -- I notice that the LiveNote for the moment says, "they were split up in chiropractors," but general panic, you say, prevailed. What did these groups of three do?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, people running all around, there was shooting, there were killings. And I think that during those two days, more killings were committed, during those two days and two nights, that is, than during the preceding three months, actually, from when the war situation started, if I can put it that way, in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. On the same day, that is to say, between the 20th and the 21st, many people were killed. Also the next day. A large number of people were killed, not only in the town of Bosanski Petrovac, in the centre of town, but also in the villages where Bosniaks lived. We talked about Rasinovac and Bjelaj. So this number far exceeded the number of victims during the intimidation period, as we call it, that is to say, the wartime period from the month of June until the month of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, how was it that all -- or the majority of the Muslims then left the municipality on the 24th of September? Was that by choice or was that by order?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, absolutely no choice. The Muslims didn't have any choice. But I feel that they could hardly wait for this kind of a call. It came from the police, the military police. They used a loudspeaker. They were driving in a vehicle through the streets where the Bosniaks lived, and they said that all the Bosniaks could take everything they could carry, all their personal belongings, and they should meet at the gasoline station, by the hotel, and that they would be transferred to Travnik, to Central Bosnia, and that's exactly what happened. A long column of Muslims, Bosnian Muslims, from Bosanski Petrovac, arrived in this plateau then. Trucks were already waiting, trailers, and also a small number of buses. I don't know exactly which number this involves, but everything was ready to transfer the Muslims. Of course, everybody had to pay for their tickets as well, and the tickets amounted to 50 Deutschmark. I think that almost 99 per cent of the Bosniaks of Bosanski Petrovac left Bosanski Petrovac on that day, or rather, were expelled from Bosanski Petrovac on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what route were you taken to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, along the road between Bosanski Petrovac and Kljuc and then Mrkonjic Grad, in the direction of Crna Rijeka, leading from the road towards Banja Luka, Karinovac, then the intersection, or rather, across the bridge, the Vrbas bridge, in the direction of Skender Vakuf, and of course across the Vlasic plateau, somewhere to the line, what they said was the separation line. However, I noticed that the separation line was much lower as regards the Bosniaks who were there at that position. So they were unloaded from the trucks and we were told to go away, not to look anywhere and not to deviate from that road, because there were hills and mountains on either side, and then we went in the direction of Turbe -- and what was the name of this other place? Yes, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So for the last part of your journey, were you on buses or did you have to walk?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This last part amounting to 20 kilometres, we had to cover that on foot, that is to say, we didn't have any kind of transportation, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you were sent off to complete your journey on foot, on the bus that you were on, were any of you searched or anything taken from you by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I was not on the bus. I was in a truck that had a trailer too. My entire family was there as well. Well, I personally did not have such an experience, because we had bad luck on the way, if I can put it that way. We were stopped two or three times, and we lost perhaps two or three hours on account of that. Because the brakes broke down on that particular truck. And we arrived at the line where we were supposed to be taken off. We were the last ones. I was there around midnight. However, those who arrived during the course of the day were indeed exposed to brutal attacks. They had their valuables taken away from them, watches, jewellery, rings, chains, et cetera. Of course, they were threatened by firearms that pointed at their children. That's the way they extorted these valuables from people, money and jewellery, namely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just look, please, at P1861. This is a list, apparently, of people who -- of peoples; of persons who sold real estate in the municipality of Petrovac. Do you know people on this list, and can you indicate, if we look at the first page, which, if any, you knew?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I practically knew all of these people. We're a small town. We all knew each other, practically. Quite a few of us are even related, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did any of those people who you know sell their property?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one sold their property. Absolutely not. This has to do with what we discussed a while ago, those contracts and the making of lists of persons who were supposed to go through this exchange of property to the area of Bihac. By your leave: These people really did have contracts that were signed, contracts with representatives of the Serb people from the area of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did anybody make it to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those who had left before the 27th of May. And of course, a group that went through the International Red Cross. This group consisted of some 30 to 40 passengers. They went to the territory of Bihac in order to have their families reunited. They went from Bosanski Petrovac to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after that convoy of the 24th of September, how many Muslims, roughly, were left in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the figure is between 70 -- 60 and 70 Muslims, or rather, Bosniaks, who either had something to do with the Serb army, I mean they were mobilised, or there were old men who could not leave, or they had family members in the area of Banja Luka, people who lived in Banja Luka at the time, that is. So they thought that in this way, they could reach Banja Luka. A number of them actually managed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've seen, through looking through these documents, that throughout October, or in October, the municipality was -- the Crisis Staff was reporting to issue decisions in relation to Muslims in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1853, 1854, 1855, all in fact dated the 28th of October and all effectively repeating earlier orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know of any Muslims who at that stage, for example, still had their weekend cottages in the Ostrelj settlement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that I've already answered that question. There were no Bosniaks up there. They did not reside there. They still had, owned, their property up there, but they did not go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honours look at 1857, which is behind divider 52, you'll see that it's the original decision of the 18th of June, but it seems to have been re-issued again on the 28th of October. And all the ones before that, they're all the same day, the 28th of October, and effectively they are literally word for word, although they are not quite as obvious as that for the earlier decisions. And 1859, Petrovac public security station is hereby instructed to increase patrols in areas where large numbers of Muslims live, and especially -- I'm sorry. Perhaps Mr. Hidic, could you have that, 1859.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the 28th of October, were there any Muslims left in the Bjelaj local commune?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some of them in the local commune of Bjelaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hidic, thank you very much for your patience. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Now, Mr. Hidic, you will recall that when you started giving evidence here last week, I had explained to you something which I attach great importance to, and that is that you are a witness here with a duty, a responsibility, an obligation, to answer, as fully and as truthfully, each question that is put to you, irrespective of who is putting the question to you. In other words, now you're going to be cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham for -- who is defending Mr. Brdjanin, and the obligation that I mentioned to you, that I referred to just a couple of minutes ago, applies to what you're going to be questioned upon now. You have no right to make any distinction between the Prosecution and the Defence. Your duty is to answer each and every question that will be put to you by Mr. Cunningham. You will be protected if inappropriate questions are put, and you will be allowed not to answer a question only if we say so; otherwise, your duty is to answer each and every question. Mr. Cunningham, it's in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honour, may I move down here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Please do. Make sure that the audio system is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Go ahead, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, I believe you told us that you are related to Mithid Hidic [sic], who is now the mayor of Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirsad Hidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: M-i-t-h-i-d, Mithid [sic], that's how I pronounce it. I apologise if I'm not pronouncing it correctly.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may say, Mithad [phoen] Hidic is my relative, but this relationship is not close. We are not close relatives. And if you will also allow me, he is no longer mayor. He was the mayor during the period between 1995 and 1997. That was during the transition period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You are active in the local party, the local political party, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
