utterances.text: You need to specify which party, Mr. Cunningham, because I believe there's more than one party.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Which party are you active in, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Action, or SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what is your position within the SDA?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Currently I am the president of the Executive Board of this political party in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And very briefly, sir, tell me what that job entails. What are your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify what you mean by your question? In what terms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are your functions, in other words? What are your responsibilities as president of the SDA Executive Board in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am the president of the Executive Board and I'm also the president of the municipal organisation on the territory of Bosanski Petrovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does that mean? A municipal organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sort of a civic council or local council, or what -- maybe a matter of translation, of interpretation, but I don't understand what a municipal organisation is. It's too generic a term. Are you referring to the local council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Executive Board is a body, an executive body, that is, and that is above the organisation in the municipal body. It is composed of the representatives of the citizens from Bosanski Petrovac who are all its voluntary members.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the materials given to us by the Prosecutor, there are a number of statements, and you've had the opportunity to read the statements that you gave to the investigators; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There is one statement from 11 November 1999. Does that sound right? Your first statement.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There is a second statement of 16 July 2000. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Could you tell me the circumstances, how it was that you gave the second statement on 16 July 2000. And let me try to clarify the question. Did you go seek out representatives of the Prosecutor's office to give this statement or did they come to you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they came to Bosanski Petrovac. They looked for me and I responded to that, if that is what you mean, how this meeting came about, that is, my meeting with these people, the representatives of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when they came to your town and sought you out, what did they ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I know that they asked me questions, that I answered those questions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did they tell you that they needed more clarification in your statement, they wanted more information? Did they make any statements along those lines?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I believe that there were questions along those lines as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I also have access to, and I want to ask you if you remember, your statement of 30 July 2003 [sic], where you provided some clarification to your earlier statements. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise to you, sir. You made some clarifications in your statements on 30 July 2001. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we had one meeting. I don't remember whether this was in 2001. And when I was shown this document, there were some corrections regarding some of the previous questions that I had answered. I don't know whether the mistakes were up to me or the recording of that statement. And those were all really minor corrections, involving some names of some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You were then brought to The Hague and you met with the Prosecutors before you testified. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And there was another statement, a very short statement, that was produced to us following your meeting with the Prosecutor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's actually incorrect. The statement was made before he had a meeting with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What I'm -- to get right to the point, Mr. Hidic, on the 21st of May, 2003, you made a statement in your native language about additional information. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I handed over some of the documents that I had brought with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Those are the only four written statements -- or let me rephrase it. Are those the only four written statements that you have made regarding the events that you have testified about?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never counted them, but I believe that I had four meetings with the Prosecutor, so I believe that four statements have ensued from these meetings that I've had in the past period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Have you made any statements, other statements, in connection with interviews with anyone other than the Prosecutor or a representative of the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned that on my arrival in Travnik in 1992, I gave a statement to some international representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let me ask the next question. Prior to your testimony, have you met with any other person other than the Prosecutor or a representative of the Prosecutor's office to discuss your case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which case?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: To discuss -- excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: To discuss your testimony in this case.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I have met before -- can you please explain? I don't think I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it may help if you make it clear, if it's made clear whether you mean a person in authority, some kind of authority in BiH, or what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham. You can go direct [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, have you discussed your testimony that you were about to give in this case with, for example, your friends back home in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss this, but we discussed the things that took place in Bosanski Petrovac every day. I don't know whether -- who you have in mind specifically, but what I can tell you, that we have daily conversations about that at all levels. We talk amongst ourselves, we talk at the local forum of administration, so every day we talk about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we are interested in knowing is whether anyone you may have discussed with the fact that you were going to come here and give testimony, give evidence, whether you actually went into details, whether you were told what to say, whether you were influenced in any manner, whether you were reminded about things that you should mention or not mention. Did you discuss the fact that you were going to give evidence here and the substance or the would-be substance of your evidence with anyone, be it individuals, be it authorities, whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand the question. When the Defence counsel put this question to me, I did not understand it properly. So now I can answer that I have not had any contacts or conversations about the testimony that I was to give here. So no, I have not discussed my testimony with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know if you have your very first 11 November 1999 statement available.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If he doesn't, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- usher, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: -- have it tendered to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Give him all the four statements straight away, to spare us having to come --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are three, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are four.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are four. It's a mystery to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Actually, the fourth one that I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Three in 1999 -- 06/07/2000, 30/07/2001, and the last one of the 21st of May

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the same -- it's the 92 bis. There are only actually three statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It was simply to -- he attested to the truth of the contents and made some changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, if you could go to your very first statement, that is your statement of 11 November 1999, the very last -- I believe it's the very last paragraph of that statement. And I'm going to read a paragraph from it, and I just want to get your comment on this. I believe that the end of that statement says: "I was doing research on these things that happened in Bosanski Petrovac in the cause of my duties. It was putting things into chronological order, locating witnesses, et cetera." I believe that's the very last entry on your statement, 11 November 1999. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an explanation that had to do with the war period, when I had the opportunity to collect the statements of the eyewitnesses leaving the territory of Bosanski Petrovac. So this has to do only with the war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What I think I heard you say is that that statement has to do with the fact that while you -- when you returned to Bosanski Petrovac, one of the things that you did was go to the government buildings and look for and collect documents. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned to Bosanski Petrovac, I had the opportunity, and I had access to the Bosanski Petrovac municipality building, and there I found all the documents that were left behind in the archives of that building in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I believe you told us that that wasn't your immediate concern when you returned to Bosanski Petrovac, that those documents came to you after about a month.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned, or a month after the return of the citizens of Bosanski Petrovac returned in an organised manner, and that is something I was in charge with, I went to the municipal building every day. That's where my work took me, and that work was of humanitarian nature. I was the coordinator of issues, humanitarian issues, and obviously I had access to these documents, and people knew about that, but not because I collected these things for somebody. I asked for these documents for my own personal needs, to complement the things that I had already recorded during the war. I wanted to compare what I heard from the eyewitnesses with these other documents. I wanted to arrive at the truth for my own personal reasons. I was not instructed to do so, because there were already bodies which were already dealing with those issues in a very specific way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The documents that you have provided to the Prosecutor's office, including those documents that you brought with you to The Hague, were those the only documents that you collected upon your return to Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not the only ones. This is just one source, one office, or one archives. Some people who had had access to these materials came to me, brought them to me, because they knew I collected them, and that's why I recorded on the top, on the front page of every document, in the order in which the sessions had taken place. I filed them as I received them from the people who had gotten hold of them. This was accessible to everybody. The archives was accessible to everybody, because it was not under a lock; it was not safeguarded by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I take it you collected many, many documents upon your return to Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that there were many documents. I mostly collected the things that I was interested in, or some newspaper articles. There were many such articles printed in Bosanski Petrovac, but I only collected those that interested me, in order to find out what was going on in Bosanski Petrovac after we had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to change topics on you. I want to ask you a question. You've been shown, and you obviously know about the layout, the map, that is, Bosanski Petrovac. How far is Bihac from the city, the town of Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 54 kilometres exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac does not share a border with Croatia, but can you tell us how far it is from the centre of town in Bosanski Petrovac to the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian border? I never measured that distance, but along the Una valley towards Lapac and Kulen Vakuf, I believe that this is the shortest road towards Bosanski Pravac [phoen], or maybe not the shortest road, but the shortest as the crow flies, that is, between Bosanski Petrovac and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And tell us how far that is, roughly.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is up to 35 kilometres, obviously, if you take the road, then it is a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when did the hostilities, when did the actual combat fighting start in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1991, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what month?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I believe that it was in the second part of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to take you back now to 1990 and 1991, because you've told us about how things started changing in Bosanski Petrovac, and I want to ask you about some of the things that you saw and heard. The first area that I want to talk to you about is how, in the late 1980s and early 1990s, you started seeing and hearing about a number of rallies being held by Serbs and the political parties associated with the Serbs. One of the things that you told us that was happening was there was an attempt or discussion to exhume bodies of Serb partisans who had died fighting the Nazis during the Second World War. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And there were -- I believe you told us that there were rallies and meetings dealing with that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The move to exhume the bodies, was that an effort to have these individuals buried, buried in a manner consist with their religion?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You certainly didn't oppose that, did you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You talked about how at these rallies dealing with the partisans who died fighting in World War II, you talked about the rallies. Did you ever hear or become aware of the fact of the accused speaking at any of those rallies?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you not to mention the partisans, because this is not about partisans; it is about the representatives of the Serb people, as has been said, allegedly. But I must say that there is the other part of the truth, namely, that in this pit, along with the bones of the Serb civilians who were killed in 1941, and in some other years, there are the bones of their representatives of some other ethnic groups, primarily Croats, and also Muslims who were brought there and killed. So this is not only a pit containing the bones of the members of one ethnic group. The bones of others were there too. Of course, historical facts point to that, and they were kept silent about in the preceding period. So please do not mention the partisans, because the partisans absolutely - how should I put this? - partisans were not killed there and not thrown into that pit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, but my question was: At any of these rallies dealing with the exhumation, did you hear the accused speak or hear of him speaking at any of these rallies? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, if this has to do with the accused who is sitting here in this courtroom, I can say that I did not, and I cannot claim that the accused was not present. I don't know about that. But to the best of my knowledge, he did not speak there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me talk to you about SDS rallies. During this time period, other than -- let me rephrase. In addition to the rallies involving the exhumation of the bodies, the SDS also had rallies in anticipation of the election that was forthcoming?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The SDA also had rallies as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And at those rallies, would it be -- and you attended those rallies, did you not?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Both rallies. If you are talking about the founding rallies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And at those founding rallies, the SDS, their representatives, discussed what they could do to help their constituents; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this founding rally - and I am talking about the founding rally - was absolutely not dealing with what the SDS would do. The rally was used for something quite different. Guests who participated in the rally said some words that were absolutely terrifying, and it was quite clear to every citizen in Bosanski Petrovac at the time that major changes had taken place that would indeed have effects that were corroborated by the future that followed. Very little reference was made to crucial issues, like what they would do when they would come to power in terms of the economy or what they would do in terms of further developing the political system, if compared to the one that existed beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Part of what -- you told us that there were changes with the election, with what happened after the election, and one of the things that you told us changed was you started to see less channels on TV. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I believe you told us that what had happened is stations from, for example, Sarajevo and other places, could not be received in Bosanski Petrovac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That was one event or one thing that limited the amount of news and programming and information that came from the TV. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came from one direction only, that is to say, the Serb media.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You had less channels. You also saw -- another reason you saw less TV is because there were problems with the electricity, there were some power outages, where at times you couldn't get radio or TV. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since Ostrelj was destroyed in 1991, there were only two programmes that had to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was BH programme 1 of the Sarajevo television, programmes 1 and 2. They went through Ostrelj only. Of course, some citizens from Bosanski Petrovac could also follow the HTV programme that came from the transmitter at Pljesevica. There were very few people who could follow the TV programme broadcast via Kozara. There were very few. Perhaps some people could in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac follow that programme as well. I mean, this is due to the altitude, the varying altitude in different parts of the municipality -- I beg your pardon. Radio Sarajevo. It was very hard to hear that, even in normal times. But starting from 1991, it was very, very hard to hear Radio Sarajevo, and by 1992 it had become virtually impossible. But we could hear Belgrade so clearly. We could follow it during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Here's my point, and I think you told us this earlier: During this time period what you started to hear was primarily Serbian broadcasts that you characterised as very pro-Serbian. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent to which we could follow the Serb programme, until we lost that too, that is to say, until there was no more electricity, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In one of the examples that the Prosecutor showed you was example P1811. If we could show that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: 1811, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you remember looking at that exhibit, Mr. Hidic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I believe you told us there was no date on this. And if we look at the face of the document, there is no date. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You don't know when this was broadcast, but would you agree with me that it would make sense, by looking at the face of the document, that it had to have started -- it had to have been broadcast after the start of the fighting with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot say. I cannot give an answer to this question, because indeed I see this from a textual point of view, but I really never had the opportunity of hearing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I would like, with the Court's permission, to show you another exhibit, which is P1834. We know by looking at the face of this document that it is a -- it's dated 18 June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of June. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And it appears to me that it is a directive from the Bosanski Petrovac Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff to the radio station, telling them to broadcast text and music to raise the combat readiness of the Serb people. Do you see where that says that in that document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this could be heard over the local radio, that a turnaround had been made as far as this local station was concerned, while I managed to follow this radio station. That was its point, not only to raise morale, but how should I put this? - there was an ethnic thrust, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham and Ms. Korner, I have arranged with the interpreters and the technicians have very kindly agreed that we sit for a further ten minutes so that we recover the ten minutes we lost earlier when I was not feeling well. So I thank the interpreters and the technicians, and you can go ahead until 20 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The last two documents that I've shown you, Mr. Hidic, would you agree with me that these documents are pro-Serbian, as you put it, that they had an ethnic thrust to them? Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you expect me to give that kind of answer, I really cannot give an answer to that question. I mean, on the basis of these two documents, I cannot really say that they are nationalist. They have a completely different role. They are of a different nature. And of course, somebody did use them at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You would agree with me that they were directed to the Serbian population, rather than the Bosniak population or the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. Of course. Of course. That's as clear as daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in there, it talks about combat and fighting for Serbian survival and things like that; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see from the first proclamation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And wouldn't it make sense to broadcast information like this over the radio when the vast majority of the people in the army at this stage were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The Bosnian population in the vast majority -- excuse me, the Bosniak population, the Muslim population, in the vast majority of cases, had declined to be mobilised. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in your statements, you talk about the mobilisation that happened during the early 1990s and in 1991. Do you remember those statements in your written statements that you gave to the Prosecutor? Do you remember talking about mobilisation in your statements?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much I talked about mobilisation, but it's possible that I did mention it, and it's possible that I did make some statements to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, if you need to refresh your recollection about those statements, they're up there, so please take your time, because I'm going to ask you some questions about that. So if you need to, please look at the statements to refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening, can I just raise one matter in respect of this document. This is one of the documents that objection was taken to by Mr. Ackerman, on the grounds that it came from AID and that it wasn't signed or stamped. Your Honour, it's now being used, I gather, to assist the defence case, and I'm taking it that it's accepted as an authentic document; otherwise, the questions make no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, we're not waiving any prior objection that we may have made. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 16304 to 16315.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I know it's not Mr. Cunningham, because it's not his objection, but I just want to make this point for about the 999th time. Sweeping objections are made to the admissibility. It is suggested that anything that comes from AID potentially is forged, it's not signed or sealed, it's potentially an invention. Then what happens is, what's contained in the document is put to the witness as though it's the truth, and accepted. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are stepping into an area which we will definitely --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because obviously what you are mentioning is something that we will definitely have to take into consideration when we will later on evaluate the objection that the Defence raised against all documents coming from AID. Because as you well know, there could as well be some documents coming from AID which are absolutely without any trace of tenderability or whatever, others that -- what use has been made of these documents by the Defence, if any, will, of course, carry its weight, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the only point that I'm trying to make is that it's almost impossible to sort out, when one is looking at the transcript after that, without going back to look at the objections, if the Defence carry on by saying: We object to all of this. There's no value to all of this. And then use the documents to put the contents to the witness, clearly accepting what's said. And I really, for, again, I say for the 999th time, I invite Mr. Ackerman to consider carefully before issuing these blanket objections, whether they're justified, and in the event that the documents are to be used by the Defence, to at least make it clear that they're withdrawing their objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I proceed, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, I asked you to look at your statements to refresh your recollection with regard to the statements you made about mobilisation. I want to talk to you about that. At this time that we're talking about, 1990, 1991, the military obligation extended to all, irrespective of whether they were Bosniak, Croat, or Serb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's the way it was from the very outset. But let me tell you one thing: Mobilisation is something that people were dealing with in Bosanski Petrovac, say, two years prior to the outbreak of the war, perhaps even before that. They started dealing with mobilisation a lot earlier, before all these things were said in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, during the critical period that we're talking about, 1990 and 1991, you've already told us that the vast majority of Bosniaks did not respond, did not agree to be called up to mobilisation. Right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that's right. The public was aware of the fact that the presidency of the state, or rather, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, did not approve of mobilisation, did not approve of that mobilisation that was being carried out at that time. Military conscripts who were Bosniaks probably took advantage of that, and therefore did not report to units that were mentioned in their call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And there would be consequences under the law for someone who didn't respond to the call-up, someone who did not respond to mobilisation. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was said that there would be consequences, but it never happened that anybody was personally held accountable for not having responded to the call-up; at least, I am not aware of any such thing having taken place in Bosanski Petrovac, that either a Serb or a Bosniak was held accountable for not responding to the call-up. Because in the beginning, neither of these two ethnic groups responded to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Are you aware of anyone that lost their job, especially anyone who had a government job, for failing to respond to the mobilisation order?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this happened in 1992, when there was general mobilisation, or rather, when there was an order concerning mobilisation, and it primarily came from the Serb leadership, and it had to do with mobilisation. But I'm talking only about the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So I don't know if you ever answered my question. Are you aware of anyone who lost their job for failing to be called up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered before. He said: Of course, this happened in 1992. So he did answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I just didn't take "of course" as an answer, as an affirmative. If I could show the witness P1815.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If we look at that exhibit, Mr. Hidic, doesn't that exhibit reflect that - and this is maybe in the second paragraph down - that there are penalties under the law for those who -- for conscripts who fail to respond to mobilisation? Is that reflected in the middle of that document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what this document says, and I believe that this was carried out, in part, but later on. As for the number of persons who were called up to Knin, Zeljava, and Bihac, this is the territory of Croatia, and that is why people avoided responding to that call-up. They were trying to avoid going to these particular areas. Zeljava is an airport near Bihac, and this is the territory of Croatia. Of course, Bosniaks were trying to avoid that. They avoided going to such units. But there were cases when people, due to this imperative that was mentioned here, that is, the possibility of criminal prosecution, that they actually did go to these units. When we're talking about 1991, the end of 1991, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, you had indicated you wanted to go to 12.40, and this is a perfect starting point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break now, resuming at 2.00, and we'll sit right through to 4.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please take a seat. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hidic. When we left, we were talking about the changes that you saw in your hometown, your municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, and I want to talk about something else you spoke about with the Prosecutor last Thursday, and that has to do with how, in your view, Bosniak men and women were losing their job. Before you came up -- I requested that the usher tender Exhibit P1819 to you, and to refresh your recollection, and I want you to take your time to look at this, my notes reflect that that is an exhibit in which Dragan Milanovic moved to have the directors of the power supply company, the director the veterinary station and the director the post, telegraph, and telegram all be removed. Do you remember, first of all, last Thursday, talking about this exhibit and this event?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I believe you told us that all three of the directors were Bosniaks; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And only two of the three were removed, and the director of the post, telegraph, and telegram remained because, and I'm going to use your words, he was an expert. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said because he was an expert, so indispensable. But also because he was married to a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to say the same thing. It's page 50 of the transcript of last Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Hidic, this was an example of a Bosniak man keeping his employment, at least in part, because he was an expert in his field?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that you are partly correct. But in any case, before the month of June or early in June he was replaced by a Serb, who was also an SDS member, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in your days and months looking at documents in Petrovac, did you find anything that corroborated that, any documents that would corroborate what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that by the end of June of 1992, no Bosniaks worked in Bosanski Petrovac. They did not have an employment in any of the services, ranging from janitors to doctors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you did not answer the question. You did not answer the question. The question was whether you had -- whether you found any documents proving or testifying to the termination of the employment of this person and to his substitution by a Serb. Did you come across any document which referred to these two events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There are the minutes of the Crisis Staff, which deal with that and which says that the former director was replaced by Mr. Sokunovic, and this document indicates the exact time, the exact date when this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And is that a document that you brought with you from Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is among the documents that I brought with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we looked at it. It's one of the documents that we looked at on Thursday. I'll try and find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Following up on what you just said, I believe you just told us that after a certain date, there were no Bosniaks in any position in Petrovac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk about you and the head of finances. Now, I believe you told us that you worked until mid-June of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you were told, sometime in mid-June, simply not to return to work; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The man who came to collect the keys from me told me exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you ever asked to take a loyalty oath to the government?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Exhibit P1876, decision of -- Mr. Mersad Knezovic [phoen], present acting manager of PTT. Krjac Petrovac [phoen] is dismissed from duty. Sokunovic [phone] from Petrovac is appointed to PTT, and so on, acting manager in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I had asked you if you had to take a loyalty oath. You told me that you didn't. I'd like you to look at Exhibit P1837, and this has to do with the dismissal of Senada Mehdin, and if I've mispronounced that, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a problem. I have difficulties reading this because the part where the name is mentioned is somewhat blurred, and there are black stains over that part, so I have difficulties reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: You know, either from your personal knowledge and conversations with her or from what you've heard from someone else, that she was sacked. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that was around the end of June/mid-June, something in that time frame, of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Because you couldn't read the document, because it might have been blurred, I want you to assume with me that the document said that she had been discharged because she did not want to swear a loyalty to the government, okay? Assuming that, would it make sense to have someone like the head of financing or accounting for the government doing a vital function during wartime if she wasn't loyal to the government?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how she found employment. Her job was not advertised. That's where she found herself when the war started, so I cannot really give you a concrete answer. But I am aware of the fact that she was dismissed, and she didn't leave through the door. She has to jump out of the window, and she had to flee when she was leaving her job, so it was not her walking out, but jumping out of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Are you telling us that people like Ms. Mehdin - and I apologise again with the pronunciation - and other people, for example, like yourself, were simply terminated, fired, sacked, whatever the word may be, because you were Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive a piece of paper about my -- I didn't sign anything. I did not receive any notification about my dismissal. The only thing that I saw was my workbook that I found in the factory after the war, and in that workbook it said that I stopped working on the 4th or on the 5th of April. But I still claim that I never received an enactment, a piece of paper, a document that I would have signed and that would have had anything to do with my work or my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Earlier you said: Everyone, from janitors to doctors, every Bosniak from a janitor to a doctor, eventually lost their job. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I believe - and correct me if I'm wrong - I believe you are suggesting to us that, at least in part, or a large part of the reason for that, was because you were in fact Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about this time frame we're talking about, where Bosniaks are getting sacked and terminated, 1991 to 1992. Thinking back to 1991 and 1992, how was the economy in 1991/1992 compared to, say, 1987, 1988? Was it better in 1991, 1992 or worse in 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to give you a precise answer, because I'm not an economist. I know very little about that. But after the multiparty elections, the situation did not improve in my town. The situation was the same. I did not notice any particular changes that would benefit the citizens. The only changes that happened were the ones that eventually resulted in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, and the war -- the war that starts with Croatia, would you agree with me, when that war starts, the war with Croatia, it affects the local economy in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it did have a certain influence, not only on Bosanski Petrovac but also on the entire former Yugoslavia. There were certain changes, first in Slovenia, then in Croatia, and obviously this all led to major changes all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, let's focus in on the economy in Bosanski Petrovac. What the war in Croatia did was affected adversely, the economy got worse. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've already said that I'm not a good economist, that this is not my particular forte. But I've also said that I did not notice any improvements, and I believe that this is what you asked me here, that this is what your previous question was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm not asking for an economist answer. I'm asking for an answer from someone who watches what happens in his community, sees what's happening with people at their jobs. Isn't it true, when the war with Croatia starts, a number of people - Croats, Serbs, and Muslims - all are affected by the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me help you, Mr. Cunningham. As the war progressed and as matters got worse, the war with Croatia, as matters got worse -- I remember reading through your statement that you said that initially Bosanski Petrovac was not in any way affected by the war, but then, as things started changing, then things really got worse, even in Bosanski Petrovac. You've stated that you did not notice any improvement in the state of the economy, generally speaking, in your town. As we go along, as we proceed in time, did businesses start to close down? Did the economy, in general, suffer? Were people better off or better -- or worse off as a result of the war? The state of the economy in general, did it -- certainly it did not register as any progress. You have already told us that. But did it register any setback?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we focus on 1991 and on 1992, of course there was a regress in that direction, because the exchange of commodities changed. It was not the same as it used to be. And at this time, it was mostly connected with the area of Republika Srpska, and at that time I believe that this was already the case, and a lot of trade was with the Serbian Vojvodina, with which Bosanski Petrovac had traditional economic relations. As far as the economy is concerned, the product that the economy, Bosanski Petrovac, relied on was timber and timber product, but the situation changed at that time. Sipad was no longer the major player on the market. There were now new private entrepreneurs, other persons from the political top which engaged in these activities instead of the state-owned companies or previously incepted enterprises, and they did not use the former channel of distribution, the ones that used to exist from Sipad, Bosanski Petrovac, to other parts of the market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would you agree with me or not that a number of people, be they Bosniaks, Serbs, or Croats, were put out of their jobs because of the economy in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Let me change topics. One of the things you talked about on Thursday, one of the things that concerned you, was the increased presence of the military in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac. Do you remember talking about that with us last Thursday?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise for stepping on the translator's answer. You also told us -- talked about weapons in Bosanski Petrovac, and I'm going to talk to you about those two areas. You talked to us last Thursday or testified last Thursday that the Bosniak community was directed, ordered, to turn in firearms. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How did you hear about the order that came from the government, the local government, to turn in the firearms?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a public order. It was an ultimatum, and it was made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when you heard this public order, did you gather up whatever weapon or weapons you have -- and you turned it in. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not me personally, because I did not possess any firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. My mistake. I apologise. Now, earlier you told us that you were becoming very concerned about the situation that was developing in Bosanski Petrovac. I take it you were concerned for your safety?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My concern was always personal concern for the safety of my family and for my own safety, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that was a concern that many other Bosniaks had as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your testimony, as well as in your statement, you talked about the 1991 census figures for Bosanski Petrovac, showing a little over 15.500 people. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I believe you told us that a little bit over 20 per cent, I believe you told us 22 per cent of that 15.500 were Bosniaks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 22.1 per cent exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Of that 22.1 per cent out of the population of the municipality that were Bosniaks, not one of those 31 -- over 3.000 people, not one of those 3.000 Bosniaks kept a weapon? Is that what you've told this Court?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I meant to say before this Trial Chamber. What I wanted to say is that there were hunting rifles and that there were other types of firearms as well, and this is what I said. So there was a possibility to obtain all sorts of firearms through illegal channels, and these firearms, as a rule, came from the front line. It was registered, and as a rule, it was compromising for those who would purchase it from those who were selling it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And my question is very simple: Are you -- and it's just this: Based on what you saw, what you heard, you're not aware of any Bosniak who didn't comply with the order? Every Bosniak turned in their guns is what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was not in that direction. I just confirmed what I said here on Thursday in relation to the problem of weapons and disarmament, I mean the way in which the disarmament took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise, Mr. Hidic. It's probably the way that I'm asking the question. This will be my last try. Are you aware of any Bosniaks who didn't comply with the order to turn in any sort of firearm?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. You told us on Thursday, as well as in your statements, that before 1991, in your municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, there were no military installations, there were no active-duty military, and there were only reserves and TO in the area. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that started, that changed, especially in 1992 that caused you alarm, because you started seeing more soldiers, particularly Serb soldiers, at active-duty reserves at installations that had been established in your municipality. Right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say Serb soldiers. I said the army, the former Yugoslav People's Army, coming from the area of Croatia. They came to Bosanski Petrovac too, and I think that I said that Bosanski Petrovac was an important centre in that part of Bosanska Krajina. And I saw these endless columns, motorised columns, of the Yugoslav People's Army going to Jajce, Banja Luka, and of course in the direction of Drvar, and then via Drvar, to Knin. I think that that was my answer in response to that question. The question was put to me by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I guess the point I'm trying to make is: In 1992, it would make sense to have troops stationed in Bosanski Petrovac, the municipality, because it was close to the front. Right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the situation was already quite different. Please. We are talking about 1991, and we are talking about the Yugoslav army in the area of Bosanski Petrovac. They were taken in, and I think that this was actually a garrison that was moved, transferred, from Karlovac, came to Bosanski Petrovac, and they were in Bosanski Petrovac all the way up to Laniste, where the barracks were later. I think that this was an engineering unit or some kind of technical unit of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. But you would agree with me, agree with the general notion that it would make sense from a military standpoint to have your troops close to the front. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was deployed along the front line, but I'm telling you about what I know. I'm not a military strategist. My perceptions are very modest, and I am telling you only about what I saw, what was a visual thing, and what was accessible to every citizen. Every citizen could see things like this, namely, columns of the former Yugoslav People's Army in the area of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the checkpoints, because I think you told us, and correct me if I'm wrong, the checkpoints started being erected about 1991.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you told -- I believe in your statement, you said that the rationale, the basis for this was to prevent the infiltration of enemy troops from Croatia. Do you remember saying anything like that in your statement? And if you need to look, please do so.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to avail myself of this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, could you refer him precisely to which of the three statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm talking about his original statement of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: 10 November 1999. Let me see if I can locate it. If I may interrupt, Your Honour, I see on page 3 of the English version, 1, 2, 3 paragraphs down. And I apologise, Judge. I think that was his --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found this. Yes. Yes. I've just found this paragraph here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you read where you stated in that statement that there was the reason given was to prevent the infiltration of enemy troops from Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I knew, officially. This is what I was officially aware of. May I remind you that I was still employed at the time. I was still working and people came to the logistics centre to get food and other things. People did know what was going on in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, and they knew why this was happening. If necessary, I can even tell you an anecdote. A young man from Drvar was arrested by mistake --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me go ahead and interrupt you, because I don't think an anecdote is necessary at this point. And I don't say that to be rude to you, but here's my point, Mr. Hidic: I know you're not an economist, I know you're not a military expert, but you would agree with me, would you not, that it makes sense to set up checkpoints to prevent the enemy from coming in to your homeland?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. May I -- this has to do with checkpoints in Croatia. This was not that type of thing. This was only in a certain part of the area, in 1991 -- sorry -- no -- yes, it is 1991. So it's in a certain area that these checkpoints were set up. So it was not that they were set up in a war sense of the word. It wasn't like in 1992, as we were going to Grabez. Then I saw these combat checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Cunningham. Let me ask you a question, Witness. Reading through that particular paragraph of your first statement, I see that you were meticulous, you were very precise, explaining where these checkpoints were set up, and you say on the roads in Bosanski Petrovac, to Bihac, location Vrtoce; road to Drvar, location Kolunic, close to Kljuc; location Bravsko, road to Bosanska Krupa, location Krnjeusa. Would the set-up of checkpoints at these locations tally with the reason that was put by the authorities, namely, the prevention of infiltration of enemy groups from Croatia? Are these checkpoints, checkpoints that would be good for controlling -- or strategically placed for controlling, if possible, infiltrations from Croatia? Yes. I'm waiting for you, for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can say that at first, when the checkpoints were set up, they did not have that intention. The point was to control the roads. So it was only traffic control, control of normal civilian traffic taking place in that section of the road. So when this checkpoint was first set up, that was its primary task. The vehicles there were primarily trucks and passenger buses, especially the evening bus that came from the area of Sarajevo and then went to Bihac through our area, and also the other way around, from Bihac to Sarajevo. Of course, there were other civilian vehicles that were stopped at that checkpoint too. So this was one of the first checkpoints that was erected in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, and that was its purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I see it, you have already explained to us that Petrovac was -- had no border with Croatia, and I fail to understand, for example, how a checkpoint on the road from Petrovac to Kljuc could in any manner be tied up with trying to avert infiltration of enemy from Croatia, because Kljuc is to the east of Petrovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very clear, Your Honour. Bosanski Petrovac is east of Bihac. But as for the remainder of the Croatian army, near Slunj, I think that's the last town in the territory of Croatia that fell into the hands of the Serb army. So this was towards the end of 1991. Via Kladusa, via Kladusa, these people, refugees from that area, used the only possible way they took to get out. They went through Bosanski Petrovac, in transit, of course. They went to some other destination, and from there, they could be transferred to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I leave him to you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know Midho Druzic? Do you know that gentleman from Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, is it -- I believe you told us on Thursday that it was -- these checkpoints had the effect of limiting the ability of non-Serbs to travel within the municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not within the municipality; outside the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Non-Serbs were the only -- were not the only people that these checkpoints limited, because these checkpoints also limited men of military age. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you also told us that, at least early on in this process of the checkpoints, not only non-Serbs were stopped, but even Serb men, certain Serbs, were taken into custody. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that they were taken into custody. They were taken off these vehicles and were not allowed to continue their journey, those who did not have the necessary papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Both Serb and non-Serb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Ultimately, acts of violence came to your community, and I want to talk to you about those, not in detail, but I just want to make a couple of points with you. For many of the violent acts, you came upon them the following day, because they became common knowledge within your community. Right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I believe you told us of at least two deaths that were followed by funerals that were attended by both Bosniaks and Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first two killings that occurred, that's the way it was. Well, perhaps something happened afterwards too, but there were less Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You have described how, in describing for us your knowledge of some of these acts of violence, you talked about how the police would arrive, do an on-site investigation, and then basically leave. I give you the example of the gentleman who was shot and had to be buried right there in his backyard, as an instance where the police came and did just an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On-site investigation. That's what was carried out by the police, or rather, part of the police, from the police station in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And was there a concern within the Bosniak community that the police were not doing their job, not following up in trying to find out who had committed these violent acts upon the Bosniak community?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Bosniaks expected the results of this kind of investigation, but we never found out about any kind of procedure, any kind of investigation that was being carried out about the crimes committed in the territory of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that was especially true in 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Based on your observations, you would agree with me, or based on your knowledge, isn't it true that at times portions of the police, many officers in the police, would be called up to the reserves and go to the front, and go on active duty?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not everybody. There were reservists who were at the front line, but then most reservists were in town or at the checkpoints or carrying out some duties within the town or the local communes of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But a good many of them actually got called up into actual duty, actual duty at the fronts?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, no. They went to the front line every now and then. They went every now and then, and they were supposed to help out at the front line, if I can put it that way. It's not that they were permanently attached there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that every day they spend at the front line is one day less to investigate crimes in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a special team for investigating crimes, and I don't think that this was the duty of the reserve policemen, or could they do this. There were professional persons who were supposed to do that, before the war and during the war. Such persons carried out these on-site investigations at crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When talking about the destruction that came to your community, you talked about a home that had been shelled and burned, and when you went there the following day, you smelled a really, really bad odour, a chemical odour. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I talked about the attack on the Bosniak house of the Redzicis, with rifle grenades, chemical components. I talked about one house only where an attack was carried out, and in the morning, several citizens were there, and also the representatives of the political government. Let me point this out: A member of parliament was there, Dragan Milanovic. He was there. He was there. He himself, in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And of course people asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to answer -- I'm trying to help you finish today, because otherwise you will have to come again tomorrow. And Mr. Cunningham is also trying hard to finish with you today. But in order to help us help you, you need to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. You're not answering the question. You're telling us facts, some of which you had already told us before, and others which you haven't been asked to relate. The question was: Do you remember mentioning this incident? The answer should have been yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please try to answer just the question and nothing else beyond that. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And my next question is very simple. Are you suggesting that this was a chemical weapon that was used against the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I'm suggesting anything. It's a fact. There were chemical components in what was used there. I mean, let me just say this: That was the smell that could be felt, and also it could be felt in the respiratory system.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you -- have you testified briefly to the point about the work obligation that you talked about? Because you were not in the military, you were obligated, if requested to, if commanded to do so by the government, to do your work obligation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And those orders, did they typically come from the Ministry of Defence? Because I remember you testifying that the order you got was unusual. So my question is: Do the orders typically come from the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the ministry. This was the authority that worked in the field of National Defence in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And the order that you got was unusual. Tell us very, very briefly why your order -- why you felt it was unusual. Did it not come from the authority that worked in the field of National Defence in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the stamp said Titov Drvar. The stamp didn't say Bosanski Petrovac, and that's what struck me. Everything that had to do with this document had to do with Bosanski Petrovac, but the stamp came from Titov Drvar, and that was my interpretation, because this was pretty obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you know from what you saw in your municipality that many of your fellow Bosniaks, when called up to do work obligation, for example, did agricultural work during the summer; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: They also worked making the canals, working at the fish farm that was in that area as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Bosanski Petrovac doesn't have a fish farm, and that was not anything that was involved in all of this in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But the gentlemen who got called up to do their work obligation assisted in the wartime effort by helping out in the local economy. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course, because they were not employed, so they didn't do this during working hours. They were mobilised subsequently, after they had been dismissed from work. That is when they were mobilised to do this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, let's go ahead and talk about briefly -- your experience on the work obligation was the one day where you went, by transport, to an area close to the front lines, and that's when you told us that you were confronted by men in military uniforms while you were waiting on the bus. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were directly at the line. We saw each other directly, and I even knew some of the men who were there at the line then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And when the men came on the bus and started acting in a threatening and intimidating manner, it was clear to you they were upset with the Bosniak community because, in their minds, the Bosniaks were not assisting in the defence of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a group that showed up and that happily received the news that there were Bosniaks at the front line and that they were on the bus. So these were people who were quite different, who were not directly linked to the line where we were then, I mean where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm confused, because you told us that there were a group of men who got on the bus, acting threatening and in an intimidating manner. That's not the same group of people you're talking about, is it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, these are different groups. This is a group that came in motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And those people who came in motor vehicles were upset with the fact that you were a work crew, not a combat unit, ready to fight for Bosanski Petrovac. That's one of the reasons they were upset with you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not need any excuse. They did not look for any excuses. They just saw Muslims on the bus and that was good enough excuse for them to get on the bus and start taunting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: One of the ways they taunted you, one of the ways they intimidated you, was statements to the effect that the Bosniak community is not doing their fair share for the defence of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you are trying to get a different answer from me, but what I'm saying is that they didn't care whether we were putting up defence or not. The only thing that they cared about was that we were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I want to talk to you about some documents now, and believe me, I want to have you out of here by 4.00, so try to listen to my question so we can move through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the usher's permission -- with your permission and the usher's assistance, can I show him P1813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask Your Honour to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like you, in the future, you and Ms. Baruch, if possible, before proceeding with cross-examination, to give a list of the documents that you intend to make use of. This has been the practice that has been followed in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise to the Court about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. I realise that you were not informed of it. So we'll try to stick to it for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's fair, Your Honour. What I'll try to do is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, if you can hand to the usher the numbers of the documents you intend to bring forward. He will have them ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise for my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay, Mr. Cunningham. No need for that. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I believe you have Exhibit P -- excuse me, P1813 in front of you, and I believe my notes reflect that this is the decision of the Petrovac Municipal Assembly to break away from the Bihac Assembly. And I believe you testified last Thursday that your municipality had always gravitated towards Bihac. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in the reasons given in the documents for the break away from Bihac, you testified that some of the -- the reasons given were political, and if I've mischaracterised your answer, please stop me, but I believe you said that some of them were true and some of them were not true. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Tell me, very quickly, what was true, and then tell us what was not true. What was true, first of all?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to answer this question because this decision does not contain any of that; and secondly, a lot of reasons were given for which the Municipal Assembly Bosanski Petrovac had to decide to leave the Bihac region. However, one of the reasons given was an economic reason. This is totally unjustified, because the economic situation, not only in Petrovac but also in some other municipalities in the Bihac region, was very similar to the one in Petrovac. If the reason -- one of the reasons given was communications and infrastructure, then again this is not justified, because immediately before the war the waterline was completed, and in 1991, the road was being built between Bosanski Petrovac and Krupa; and this was the only road at that time that was not covered with asphalt. The complete electrical infrastructure was good. So I'm just telling you things that I can remember and that I can cite off the top of my head as reasons given by the municipality to leave the association of municipalities of Bihac. So I believe that this decision was more a political or even ethnic-related decision. It was not so much an economic or a similar decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
