utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk to you now about Exhibit P1805, that is, the Crisis Staff notes, dated 21 May 1992, covering the meeting held on 19 May 1992. And I really do want to have you out of here by 4.00. Look at that --

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be very glad if we could finish today, and I'll do my best to speed things along on my side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Just try your best just to answer the question that's posed to you, and I'm not saying this to be rude, but to remain focused on just that question. This is one of the documents that the Prosecutor talked about where there were discussions at the Crisis Staff about cattle. Do you remember the discussions about cattle?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And if you know the answer to this, agree; if you don't, that's fine too. Did you know that the cattle that are being discussed, specifically in this Crisis Staff report, were special dairy cattle that needed special attention, otherwise they ran the risk of dying very, very quickly? If you know that, fine; if not, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that these cows originated from Kupres, from a farm, a cattle-breeding farm in the territory of Kupres. They arrived in Bosanski Petrovac, so I believe that the majority of that livestock came from that area. Obviously, there were cows from other regions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me change the topic and give you a new document that you talked about, which is Exhibit P1807, 1807 is the Crisis Staff notes from May the 24th, and you've talked to us about this. And if I could, to help you try to get out of here in time, take you to the fourth page, numbers 2 and number 3. With respect to number 2, that -- there's some sort of decision, conclusion, decision made by the Crisis Staff that the ethnic Muslims can stay at work in accordance with the needs of the company. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And number 3 talks about the establishment of a military court to deal with those stealing, looting, things like that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that a court was indeed set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that would be some sort of move on behalf of the civilian authorities to deal with the looting, the lawlessness that was happening in the area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was just an attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: While we're talking about war booty, and I'm going to use the phrase that you used, I believe you testified last week - and I don't have the document in front of me - that there was a request by the Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff for assistance in dealing with the problem of stealing and looting in the area. Do you remember talking about that, generally speaking, last Thursday?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And there was an effort made to confiscate stolen property, and you told us that it had been stacked up or piled up in front of the police station. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What the police managed to confiscate from various individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. But there were -- I think you told us there were difficulties in getting it back to the rightful owner, although it had been confiscated, there were difficulties in returning it.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not what I said. That property was never returned to its rightful owners, and this is what the problem was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. If I could show, with the usher's assistance, Exhibit P1809. And in this, and if it will assist you, on page 3, it talks about the use of the public security station Petrovac, used for detaining perpetrators of criminal acts. And one of the things that you underlined there was that prisoners in custody could be used doing work for a public interest related to defensive preparations. Right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what page this is on? I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Go to page 3, towards the very bottom, number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are referring to the English version when --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's page 2, paragraph numbered 3, the third paragraph from the bottom. Are you referring to [B/C/S spoken] -- can you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And my question to you was -- is now: Having located that notation, prisoners could be used for doing work for a public interest related to defence preparations. And is that one of the things that happened in Bosanski Petrovac, that they did in fact go to help with defensive preparations?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did not happen to the prisoners in Bosanski Petrovac. The detainees did not participate in the kind of works mentioned herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, in an effort to speed this along, can I have a minute just to look through some notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you now about Prosecutor's Exhibit P1869, which are the Crisis Staff notes of June 3rd, 1992, covering the meeting of the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Petrovac of June 2nd, 1992. And on the first page of this document, under the notation that says "agenda," there are discussions -- it's number 1, and on the English version it starts on page 1 and continues to page 2, talking about how that non-Serbs be allowed to leave the territory, under the condition that Serbs -- it talks about an exchange of family for family. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And what was -- and correct me if I'm wrong. I may be wrong on my dates, but there what had happened was there was an effort to exchange Bosniak property in Serb territories, such as Bosanski Petrovac, with Serb territory in other areas. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the area was defined in those talks, and it was defined only to Bihac, and it was only Bihac that was the subject of intra-municipal talks between Bihac and Bosanski Petrovac, that is, among the top officials and top political leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in actuality, some, but certainly not all of those exchanges, took place because Bosniak families who made their way to Bihac did acquire what had formerly been Serb property?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very few Muslims from Bosanski Petrovac indeed left earlier, before this road was closed, and they went to Bihac. Gradually they moved in some of the houses. I don't know whether this was a part of the aforementioned agreement or something else, because these people were not present when contracts were being signed up in Bosanski Petrovac municipality. They had left long before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. If I could, with the Court's permission and the usher's assistance, talk with you about Exhibit 245A, which is, for the record, the minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting of 14 June 1992. In this meeting, the Crisis Staff discuss the question of the Muslim community, and I'm talking -- I don't know if my notes -- my copy shows -- I'm referring to the underlined portions that you underlined.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a copy with anything underlined in the minutes that were -- that had now been given to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise to you. This is the document that was exhibited this morning by Ms. Korner, and not the one which was in the binder before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. I know there's a lot of confusion. This was the one given to us by AID and the other ones are the ones provided by Mr. Hidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the fact that we all have this document in front of us, I'd like to ask him about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that in here, under item number 1, that the Crisis Staff talks about the Muslims who -- the Bosniaks who have pledged loyalty be included in the defensive preparations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want you to go to the page -- I believe it -- it might be your next page, but it's the portion of the document that deals with the conclusion. And in the conclusion, as we read it, that references the Crisis Staff in Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise for stepping on your answer. But it talks about requesting a session with the Crisis Staff in Krajina. Here's my question: As you were looking through the documents that were available to you in the municipality upon your return, did you try to gather every document that referenced the Crisis Staff in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. At this moment, I can't answer this question. But in any case, I did not come across any such documents that would be directly connected with the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Petrovac or the region of Banja Luka. I really did not come across the documents of that sort. I may have come across some letters or documents referring to some other documents of that kind, because even here it says the Crisis Staff, Petrovac, is going to ask the Crisis Staff of the autonomous province of Krajina. So this is what I've been talking about, the addressee is related to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But you didn't find any documents that would show, for example, in this case, that they first contacted the Crisis Staff in Krajina and then that the Crisis Staff in Krajina did anything about it? You didn't find any documents like that, did you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just a moment to talk to Ms. Baruch, because I think I'm at an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Switch off the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I have no more questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. [Microphone not activated] Thank you for the efficient way in which you conducted cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just ask one question in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see Your Honour is packing up. Only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was just clearing up papers from right in front of me because they were piling up

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, you were asked about the founding rally, do you remember, of the SDS in Bosanski Petrovac, by Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not given the opportunity to give my complete answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you: One thing you said, because it was suggested to you that what they were doing, what they were saying, was what they could do to help their constituents, and your reply, partly, was to this effect: That wasn't the case. It had very little to do with crucial issues. And you highlighted those issues. But they used some words that were absolutely terrifying. What words did they use that were absolutely terrifying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also, while you are putting this question, because this was a question that I was going to ask: He also mentions guests participating in these rallies. He uses the word "guests." I don't know whether that was a matter of interpretation or whether he really used the word "guests." If perhaps he could explain. We could go back to the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think perhaps if you can --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you talk about guests, Mr. Hidic, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I meant the presence of those people who were not locals, who were not from Bosanski Petrovac municipality, but rather, came from some other areas of the former Yugoslavia who were invited to attend that as guests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think in -- when I was asking you questions on Thursday, you mentioned people like Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, Biljana Plavsic was present after the exhumation from Rizovacka Jama. She attended a rally of people in Knosa [phoen] that was staged on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The phrase used, Ms. Korner, was guests who participated in the rally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Said some words that were absolutely terrifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can you remember who any of those guests were? If you can't, say so.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I remember, absolutely. The first honourary guest at that rally, Dr. Raskovic; then Bogdan Kecman, from the area of Kosovo, and he came with the Kosovski Bozuri; then also the travelling suite was there, that's what I called them, it was the group from Stara Pazova, that travelled all over the place and they attended practically all the important rallies that had to do with the establishment of the SDS in Bosanska Krajina. Then from Knin there was Babic. Well, right this moment, this is what I can remember. Perhaps if I had more time, I could remember far more persons. So there were guests from all parts of the former Yugoslavia. Vojvodina in particular, I would like to point out, namely, Stara Pazova, and then Belgrade, Kosovo, and Kninska Krajina, and of course Knin itself. Also from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Guess. What was said that terrified you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The speeches of some of the speakers at that rally who talked about the jeopardy of the Serbian people, that they were jeopardised by the Ustashas from Croatia and the Turks, the Muslims, and the Muslims were called to go back to their old faith, the faith of their forefathers. Otherwise, they would suffer consequences, that is to say, they would be impaled. That was what Mr. Bogdan Kecman said. Raskovic, who spoke the longest at this meeting, he spoke about the conflict that was in the offing between the Croats, the Ustashas, as he said, and the Serb people, and he said that the spectre of the Ustashas was looming over the Serb people again. I think that I managed to convey some of the words that were uttered at that rally. Although I came somewhat late, I wasn't there from the very beginning, I mean when this discussion took place with the representatives of the Serb people, even they were bitter about these impudent things that were said in front of the town church, where the stalls were set up, I mean that such words could be heard there. Yes, I just remembered now. A peoples' hero from the Second World War, Djuran Kovacevic was from Petrovac, he also gave himself the right to speak. And then a former soldier spoke, a former JNA man, Marjanovic, Stanko Marjanovic. He was one of the founders of the SDS in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac. And so on and so forth, all the way up to Rajko Novakovic, nicknamed Mujo, who was president of the SDS board eventually, and after the elections, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just two final things, and I think you may have told us before, but who was Mr. Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Raskovic was the founder and president -- I mean, I don't know which office he held exactly, but he was in very high places in that period of time, in Bosanska Krajina and in Krajina in Croatia, among the Serb people there. I think that at that rally, he was accorded very high honours, practically like a visiting head of state. There was also a horse-drawn carriage there for him. I also omitted to mention that clergymen were also present at this rally. They spoke too. But I think that their speech was more moderate, more tolerant, and it was more understandable, when compared to the speeches made by the persons that I referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Kecman, who you mentioned on a couple of occasions, do you know what position he held in 1990?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know about this man is that originally he hailed from the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, Drinic, to be more specific, since the Second World War, he had been living in Kosovo. I was told that he was the president of this association called Kosovski Bozuri. They had some sort of an important role to play in that area when they dealt with the national issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Hidic. That's all I ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Janu, who comes from the Czech Republic, would like to put -- is going to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, I have only one question for you. When you were dealing with the Prosecution Exhibit P1840 -- if the witness can have this exhibit - it was the order of public security station for isolation of the people from 1st July 1992. And when you were dealing with this document, you said you know the majority of the people on this list. Can you assist the Chamber, or clarify for us, if you know: If you look at this list, can you tell us, was this list done together, randomly, or was there any intent in other way, knowing those people, had those people some special importance or was it just random list?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as brief as possible and to give a precise answer to this question. The first person on this list, number 1, Ekrem Didovic, is the first person to be arrested in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac. He had worked in Germany for many years, and then, when he returned, he set up a company. So he worked as a businessman in Bosanski Petrovac. The other person is Zijad Ramic, Zika, again a successful businessman from before the war, a private entrepreneur, of course, in Bosanski Petrovac. Ibrahim Hrkic, he's from Bjelaj. He doesn't belong to this category of persons. 4, Husein Bajric is a man who was taken advantage of by the police. He was released. Nobody knows why, how come he was released from the camp at Kozila. After the war he was seen in the territory of Bihac, or rather the region of Bihac. Kartal Fadil, Kudja. He is also one of the private businessmen there. He had his own car repair shop and so on. Muhamed [as interpreted] Hidic is a relative of mine. He has a university degree. He worked at SIP, the SIP company. He was a reserve officer of the JNA, that is to say, the legal, legitimate Yugoslav army. And in those other papers, it can be seen that he refused orders to respond to call-up, simply because this was no longer the army that he had belonged to. Midhat Druzic is also a person from Petrovac I know very well. He was a worker at Autotransport. He's a driver by profession. And he happened to be on this list because a year or two before that he was involved in the building and repair of the mosque in Donji Biscani, which was regrettably destroyed in 1992. So I don't want to take up too much time. And so on and so forth. I think that the first 20 persons from this list happened to be entered in Bosanski Petrovac, at the prison there. The prison became too small, so then some kind of a bigger prison was made, an isolation centre, and of course people were brought into custody every day, interrogated, detained, and so on. I don't know whether I managed to answer the question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do not have questions myself, which means that essentially your testimony comes to an end here. You will soon leave this courtroom, escorted by the usher, and you will be given all the attention you require to enable you to return to your country. Only two things left for me to say. One is to thank you, on behalf of the Tribunal, and my two colleagues, Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and Judge Taya from Japan, who is absent today due to personal problems. Thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence in this trial. Last thing is to wish you a safe journey back home. You can now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you as well. I am particularly pleased to have had this opportunity to come here and to express what has been within me for years. I feel relieved in a way now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hidic. Tomorrow, Mr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. As I say, if possible, Ms. Richterova is going to be taking the witness. We'd like to be able to finish him tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I can promise you is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Hoping that I will feel a little bit better tomorrow, because I think I'm running a temperature at the moment, we'll try -- we'll start at 9.00, and if we see at any time that there is a likelihood that we might need a few more minutes, just give me the signal, because you are in a better position to gauge that, give me the signal and I'll try and see what we could do. I don't think it would be a major problem if we need to sit for an extra half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, exactly. If it looks like it's only a few minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, I would need to know, because I would need to discuss it with the interpreters and the technicians, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, but other than that it's the normal 9.00 to 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. 9.00 to 12.30, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think -- Mr. Cunningham told me that he didn't intend to be very long, and like Your Honour, I'm most impressed by the efficiency of his cross-examination. So I'm taking it that it will be -- he will be finished tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 3.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of May 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25
